activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
Kayla laced her sneakers at the kitchen table while her mom buttered toast, because today was her first day volunteering at the River Street Food Bank. "Remember when you were six," her mom said, "and you cried because we threw out the jack-o'-lantern?" Kayla laughed. She had wanted to keep it on the porch forever, and when it softened and collapsed, she had buried it under the maple tree with a popsicle-stick marker. She still couldn't stand seeing food thrown away, which was exactly why she had signed up to volunteer.

The food bank smelled like cardboard and oranges. A supervisor named Dara handed Kayla a box of donated groceries from Hartman's Market: lettuce with brown edges, apples with dents, peppers that had gone soft in spots. "Sort the good from the not good," Dara said. "Blemished is fine. Rotten is not."

Kayla worked down the row, but a question kept nagging her. These vegetables weren't rotten, they were just ugly or slightly old, and the store had gotten rid of them anyway. She counted the box quickly: forty-two items, and thirty-one were still perfectly good if you cut around the spots. That was more than half saved from the trash. She wondered how big that number would get if you counted every store, every kitchen, every school cafeteria in the whole country.

She found Dara stacking cans. "Do you know how much food in the whole United States just gets wasted, never eaten?" Dara smiled. "Actually, yes. The Department of Agriculture estimates between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted." Kayla stared. Out of every ten boxes like this one, three or four never fed anybody at all.

She wanted to test it. At home that afternoon, she pulled everything out of her own refrigerator and counted: sixty items. If the estimate held for her family too, somewhere between eighteen and twenty-four of them would end up in the garbage. She made a plan, writing it on the whiteboard by the fridge. Leftover rice became fried rice. Soft apples became applesauce. The half-onion went into soup. By the end of the week the trash can was nearly empty, and her little brother, Marcus, who usually complained about leftovers, asked for seconds of the applesauce and said it tasted better than the store kind, almost like something from the artisan bakery downtown, the way the whole house smelled like cinnamon.

At her next shift, Kayla told Dara about the experiment, and Dara gave her a new job: teaching the sorting table to keep slightly blemished fruit out of the discard bin. "You have a distinct talent for this," Dara said, handing her a permanent marker to label the rescue crate. Kayla wrote RESCUED on the side in big letters, then set a rescued apple on top, where everybody could see it.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
Owen set his pencil down and glared at the paper. His street looked like a street that had been through a landslide. The buildings on the left leaned one way, the buildings on the right leaned the other, and the road between them wandered off the page like a snake that had lost its glasses. He wanted to draw the view from his grandmother's front porch, the one she said she might have to sell, so he could give her the picture before the moving truck came. He had one week.

"You're frowning at that paper like it insulted you," his mom said, setting a lemon on the counter. She turned it over, squinted, and muttered, "Is that fungus? I think that's fungus." She dropped the whole thing in the trash and came to stand behind him.

"Perspective," Owen said. "You're supposed to make lines go to a vanishing point, and I get that, but my street won't cooperate."

His mom pulled out the chair across from him. "Did I ever tell you about the nail hole? In the Last Supper?" She waited while he shook his head. "The single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there."

Owen looked up. "A nail hole? In one of the most famous paintings in the world? You can still see it?"

"Still there."

He sat with that for a second. Strings, from a nail. Strings that stretched out from one spot to guide the lines. So Leonardo hadn't just eyeballed it, and he hadn't started with the walls or the ceiling either. He had started with the one point, the point at Christ's head, and let every line grow outward from there like spokes on a wheel.

Owen flipped to a fresh page. This time he drew nothing but a small dot first, halfway up the paper, right where the street should disappear. He pressed the pencil tip so hard it nearly poked through, then found a thumbtack in the junk drawer, set it exactly on the dot, and looped a piece of sewing thread around it. He pulled the thread taut and drew along its edge, then moved it and drew again, line after line radiating out from the tack like rays from a tiny sun.

"Why the actual thread?" his mom asked.

"Because my hand curves. The thread doesn't."

When the lines were done he took the tack away and built the street on top of them, storefronts, windows, a mailbox. The buildings stood up straight and tall. The road ran true and narrow and went exactly where it was supposed to go, shrinking toward the dot until it vanished. In the middle of the road, far down where everything converged, the paper held one small, dark pinprick where the tack had been.

Owen leaned close to it. "I'm leaving it," he said. "Grandma can find it."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
story:
Aiden carried two paper cups of punch across the community hall, scanning the folding tables for his grandmother's church group. The hall had been split in half for the interfaith evening, with hymnbooks on one side and a cloth-covered table on the other, where a Sikh family was arranging a small stand wrapped in saffron fabric. Aiden's assignment for school was due Monday: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had planned to just look things up online, but his grandmother had said the community hall evening would demonstrate more than any website could.

At the Sikh table, a boy about his own age sat copying something into a notebook in careful Punjabi letters. His name tag read Vikram. When Aiden set a cup of punch down beside him, Vikram grinned and covered his page. "You can look. It's not secret." The page was covered with lines of Gurmukhi script, the same lines over and over.

"That's a lot of copying," Aiden said.

"It's Japji Sahib. The morning prayer." Vikram tapped the notebook. "I have to know it well, because I'm getting ready for my initiation."

Aiden frowned. "Like a ceremony?"

"It's called Amrit Sanchar," Vikram said, and then his little sister tugged his sleeve and he went to help her with her shoes, leaving Aiden staring at the notebook.

Aiden wandered back to the church side, where his grandmother was stacking chairs. She had retired from the post office last spring, and now that she drew a pension, she volunteered at events like this almost every weekend. Aiden asked her what she thought happened after death, and she said what she always said, about heaven and being with God. Then she asked what the family across the hall believed.

"I don't know yet," Aiden admitted. "They said something about the soul merging with God, like a drop going back into the ocean. But I got interrupted."

He remembered then, suddenly, a funeral he had attended two years before, for his grandfather. After the service, in the church basement, a man had stood up and described reincarnation so vividly that several of the mourners had leaned forward, listening to something completely different from the minister's sermon. Aiden had been eleven and had thought the man was simply wrong. Now he wondered whether he had been biased that day, hearing only what he already expected to hear.

He marched back across the hall, punch sloshing. "Vikram. For my project. Does Japji Sahib say anything about what happens after you die?"

Vikram's mother looked up from the cloth-covered table and smiled. "Ask him what he's reciting it for," she said, and went back to smoothing the fabric.

"I'm reciting it because it's part of the ceremony," Vikram said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "And the prayer talks about the soul's journey. So I guess learning it is like practicing for the whole thing, the life after this one too." He looked surprised at his own sentence, then pleased.

Aiden wrote fast, filling half a page. "Can I ask you one more thing on Monday? After you've thought about it more?"

"Bring two cups of punch," Vikram said, and turned back to his notebook, pencil moving through the letters one more careful line at a time.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
Lea had exactly one job at the polling station: hold the "Vote Here" sign without whacking anyone with it. She was failing. The sign was nearly as tall as she was, and every time a voter walked past, the cardboard corner lunged at somebody's hat.

"I saw that," said Marcus, her best friend, who was supposed to be handing out sample ballots. "Your sign is attacking Mrs. Okafor. Again."

"The sign has a mind of its own. I'm just the camouflage, hiding its sinister plans." Lea wrestled the cardboard into a corner and propped it against the wall like a sleeping dragon.

Their civics class had sent them here to participate in Election Day, which mostly meant standing in the hallway of the community center for two hours. Their teacher, Ms. Reyes, had assigned a worksheet that Lea had stuffed in her back pocket: Read a right listed in the Constitution, then explain it in your own words. She'd been avoiding it all morning.

"Did you do the worksheet?" she asked Marcus.

"I wrote that the Constitution is a big paper that tells the government what it can't do. Very inspiring. Ten out of ten."

Before Lea could argue, a man with a clipboard hurried over. He was from the local newspaper, and he was upset. "They moved me to the parking lot," he said to the poll manager. "I need to photograph inside."

"Rules are rules," the manager said. "No cameras past this line."

Lea watched the man retreat, muttering. Something nagged at her, a pattern she couldn't quite see yet. Marcus had said the Constitution tells the government what it can't do. So what stopped the government from shutting down a newspaper entirely?

She pulled out her phone and searched. The First Amendment. She read it twice, lips moving. It protected freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. Five things, all in one amendment. The press. There it was, printed plain as a cereal box label.

"Marcus," she said, yanking his sleeve. "The First Amendment protects the press. And speech. And religion. And peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. That's why that reporter gets to be annoying at all."

"So the government can't just squish newspapers?"

"Apparently not." Lea flipped her worksheet over and wrote fast, in her own words: The First Amendment means the government can't tell people what to believe, what to say, or what to print, and it can't stop us from gathering peacefully or complaining to its face.

Marcus read over her shoulder. "Complaining to its face. Truly your finest work."

The reporter came back through the doors, camera bouncing on his chest, having negotiated a spot near the door. He raised the camera toward the check-in table, and Lea, without thinking, yanked her sign out of the corner to hold it high and proud.

The cardboard corner clipped his clipboard, and his pen flew across the floor.

"You're attacking the press now," Marcus said. "The exact press we just learned is protected."

Lea chased the pen, held it out to the reporter, and grinned. "Freedom of the press," she said. "And freedom of my sign. Somebody should write an amendment about that one."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
story:
At the first turn of the track, Madison bent to retie her shoe even though it didn't need it, because bending gave her an excuse not to look at the girl stretching beside her. That girl was Priya, the fastest eighth grader in the county, and in twenty minutes they would both toe the line for the eight hundred metres, the race Madison had bombed at twice already.

"You went out too fast last time," Priya said, not unkindly. "I watched. First lap like a rocket, second lap like a walk."

"I know," Madison said. The embarrassment still stung from the meet where she'd led at four hundred metres and then been passed by six people, one by one, her legs turning to wet cardboard. The trouble was she couldn't feel it happening. Everything seemed fine until suddenly it wasn't, which meant the problem was hidden somewhere she couldn't see, in the way she spent her energy, like a bank account draining without receipts.

Her brother Dev, who swam, had run into a version of the same puzzle last summer. "Freestyle," he'd told her, frowning at the television. "You'd think everyone would pick something different, right? Like, it's free. Any stroke you want."

"So why doesn't anyone?"

"I asked my coach. Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races, because it's the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes. It's just faster. That's the whole answer." Dev had shrugged. "But you still have to swim it smart, because if you go out too hard, even front crawl won't save you."

Madison had rolled her eyes at the time. Now, standing at the line under an ominous gray sky, the idea came back to her from a new angle. The swimmers didn't win by choosing the fastest stroke alone; they won by managing the fastest stroke. Maybe pace worked the same way. The first lap of an eight hundred wasn't the race at all. It was an investment, and if she poured everything into it, there'd be nothing left when the actual race began.

So she made a plan she could test: on the first lap she would stay three steps behind Priya, no closer, no matter how easy it felt. If the plan was wrong, she'd lose again and know it. If it was right, the second lap would tell her.

The gun cracked. Priya swept to the front, and Madison sat three steps back, her legs begging to go, the whole field stringing out behind them. Four hundred metres. The bell. Then, coming off the final turn, the gap ahead of her began to shrink, one step at a time, like the second half of a race she'd never actually run before. She surged. Twenty metres out she was even with Priya's shoulder, hearing her own breath like a drum.

"Where did you come from?" Priya gasped.

Madison didn't waste the air to answer. She just leaned forward and ran through the line.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
story:
Aiden opened the group chat for the Science Olympiad team at 7:03 p.m. and found forty-one unread messages, which was never good. The facts, as far as he could piece together from the wall of text, were these: Marcus had left his weather station project at home, Priya had told Mr. Okafor that the missing data had been collected when it hadn't, and she'd done it because Marcus had covered for her little brother the week before when the brother got caught sneaking into the gym. Everyone agreed on all of it. Nobody agreed on anything else.

"she LIED to a teacher," Devon typed. "the rest of the team worked hard on real data and she faked ours. that's a fairness thing. rules apply to everyone or they apply to no one."

"she was paying back a debt," Zoe answered. "Marcus protected her brother. you don't drop people who helped you. that's loyalty, devon, look it up."

Aiden read it twice. That was the strange part. Devon and Zoe weren't fighting about what had happened. They were fighting about what it meant, using the exact same forty-one messages as evidence. He thought about how light bends through a prism and comes out in different directions depending on the glass, how the same beam refracts into colors that weren't visible before. Same light in, different light out. He had a hypothesis: the facts weren't the problem at all. He decided to test it.

He typed: "devon, name one fact you and zoe disagree about. an actual fact."

The chat went quiet for a full minute, which in this group was like a year. Then Devon wrote, "okay. none. she did it, marcus owed her, okafor believed her. we agree."

"so you agree on every single fact," Aiden typed, "and you still land on opposite sides."

"yes???" Zoe sent, followed by the confused emoji and then, "oh."

Aiden's mom knocked on his door and said something about the weather forecast, precipitation moving in overnight, did he have his rain jacket by the door. "Yeah, in a minute," he said, because something was happening in the chat. Devon had sent a screenshot of the team rulebook, and Zoe had sent a photo of the poster in the gym that said WE TAKE CARE OF OUR OWN, and they were now arguing about which document mattered more, which was, Aiden realized, the same argument wearing a new shirt.

He tried one more test. "imagine priya covered for someone who was NOT her friend. devon, would you be madder or less mad?"

"same," Devon said.

"same," Zoe said, "but because it would be pointless loyalty."

Aiden laughed out loud, alone in his room, at two people typing "same" about opposite feelings. He typed, "wait. you both just said priya values something different than you do. devon you value fairness. zoe you value loyalty. nobody's wrong about the facts. you're not even wrong about the values. you just have different ones."

There was a long pause. Then Marcus, silent for the entire fight, finally appeared.

"guys. I'm quitting the team either way. I don't want priya taking heat for me," he wrote. "also aiden you type like a documentary narrator but you're right."

Zoe sent, "we could split into two teams. one for fairness, one for loyalty."

Devon sent, "that's the dumbest idea I've ever heard. I love it."

Aiden looked at the rain starting against his window and went to get his jacket, and when he came back there was a new chat, created by Zoe, named Team Loyalty, and another one already created by Devon, named Team Fairness, and both of them had added him at the same time.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
story:
Amelia slid her copy of To Kill a Mockingbird across the library table so the worn cover faced the circle of folding chairs. It was her turn to lead book club, and she had drafted her notes on three index cards, which now stuck together in her nervous hands. She peeled them apart and cleared her throat.

"Okay, so, symbolism," she began. "My cards say a symbol is when an object stands for a bigger idea, but I want to try something instead of just reading that. Everybody, think about the title. Why mockingbirds?"

Dev, who had eaten half a cookie already, raised his hand even though nobody needed to. "Because they're in the book? Atticus says something about them."

"That's the thing," Amelia said, flipping to the page she had dog-eared the night before. She read aloud: Miss Maudie explains that it is a sin to kill a mockingbird because mockingbirds do nothing but sing their hearts out for us. She looked up. "So they don't hurt anybody. They just give you music. And they're innocent."

Priya leaned forward, bouncing her chair onto its back legs. "So which characters are the mockingbirds? That's like a scavenger hunt."

"Exactly," Amelia said, her acute attention locking onto the circle of faces. "That's what I did last night. I made a list." She turned over the third index card. "Tom Robinson, first. He never hurt anyone, and they destroyed him anyway. And Boo Radley. He leaves presents in the tree, he saves the kids, and people made up scary stories about him for years."

"Him too?" Dev said. "I only thought of Tom."

"Try it yourself," Amelia said, grinning. "Who else just gives and gives and gets nothing back?"

The room went quiet except for the radiator clicking, which somebody had set by twisting the thermostat until the librarian came over and turned it back down. Then Marisol, who almost never spoke first, said slowly, "What about the kids themselves? Scout just... exists. She gets attacked for something her dad did."

The whole circle erupted at once, everyone talking over each other, and Amelia held up her hands. "Wait, wait, test it like a scientist. Does the person do harm? No. Does somebody try to punish them anyway? If yes, mockingbird."

Dev counted on his fingers. "Tom, yes. Boo, yes. Scout, yes. Man, this whole book is a nest of mockingbirds."

"That's the pattern," Amelia said. "The title isn't just a bird. It's telling you from page one who to watch and who's going to get hurt." She wrote the three names on the whiteboard and underlined them twice.

Priya jabbed a finger at the board. "Next meeting, can we do foreshadowing? I want to find every warning we missed."

"Bring sticky notes," Amelia said, and passed the cookies.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
story:
At dinner Jaxson slid his phone across the table before his mother could tell him to put it away. "Read this headline," he said. "Kids who eat oatmeal get better grades. It's all over the internet today."

His older sister Priya leaned over, noodles still twirling on her fork. "So we should eat oatmeal every morning? Lucky you, you already do."

"That's the thing." Jaxson set down his fork. He had eaten oatmeal almost every day since second grade, and his grades were fine, but plenty of kids in his class who ate sugary cereal had better grades than he did. Something about the headline itched at him. "I want to know how they know it's the oatmeal."

"Maybe they asked a bunch of kids what they eat and what their grades are," Priya said.

"Okay, but what else do oatmeal kids have in common?" Jaxson pushed his peas around his plate while he thought. The steam from the pot of rice fogged the kitchen window, and his father was ladling out seconds, but Jaxson barely noticed. He kept seeing the chart from the article, two lines rising together like teammates. He remembered something else with two rising lines he'd seen in a video last month. "Wait. Ice cream sales go up in summer, and sunburns go up in summer, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburns. Hot weather causes both."

"So what's the hot weather here?" his father asked, sitting back down.

Jaxson grabbed a napkin and drew two wobbly arrows pointing at the same box. He speculated out loud, throwing out ideas faster than he could test them. "Maybe oatmeal kids have parents who make breakfast, and parents who make breakfast also check homework, and that's the actual thing. Or oatmeal is cheap and fast, so maybe those families just have calmer mornings."

"That would be tedious to check," Priya said, "but you could try. Ask your class."

The next day Jaxson did an annoying but simple thing. Between classes he asked eleven kids two questions: what they ate for breakfast, and whether anyone at home helped them study. He tallied the answers in the back of his notebook during lunch, then again after school because he smudged the first page. The pattern surprised him. The breakfast foods were all over the place, cereal, oatmeal, leftover pizza, but the kids with the best grades almost all had someone checking in about school, whatever was on their plates.

At dinner he laid the notebook on the table between the rice pot and the salad. "The oatmeal might not be doing anything. Both things could be caused by something else." Priya tapped his chart of arrows and grinned.

"From your perspective, does that mean I can stop making oatmeal?" his mother asked.

"Keep the oatmeal," Jaxson said, spooning up another bite. "I just want the headline to say the true thing."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
story:
Arthur sat on the living room floor with his laptop balanced on the coffee table, two news articles open side by side. His class project was due Monday, and he had promised his partner Nadia he would find two stories about the same event so they could compare them. He had picked the downtown march from last Saturday, the one his mom had driven past on her way to the store.

The first headline read, "Thousands Gather in Peaceful Protest for Cleaner Parks." The second read, "Rioters Disrupt Downtown, Businesses on Edge." Arthur scrolled down. Both articles described the same street, the same afternoon, the same crowd. Both mentioned a broken window at a bakery and a crowd estimate near four thousand. He read them again, then leaned back against the couch and stared at the ceiling fan.

He noticed something odd. When he read the first one, he pictured people holding signs, maybe singing. When he read the second, he pictured shouting and running, even though the article said almost the same things had happened. He tested it. He covered the headline on the first article with his hand and read only the body. Then he covered the second headline and did the same. The paragraphs underneath felt almost identical. The difference was the words on top.

"Protesters," he said out loud. "Rioters." He wrote both words in his notebook, then wrote "crowd of about four thousand" between them. If a word could make him picture two opposite scenes from the same facts, that was worth putting in the project. He could deduce that the writers had chosen those words on purpose, or at least that the words did work the facts alone didn't do. He underlined the pair twice.

Nadia came over at four, dropping her backpack by the door and flopping into the armchair. He turned the laptop toward her. "Read this one, then this one. Same day, same street." She read for a minute, frowning. "The second one makes me feel like it was dangerous," she said. "The first one makes it sound like a picnic."

"That's the thing," Arthur said. "They're loaded words." She raised an eyebrow, and he pointed at the screen. "Same crowd, but the word choice pushes you one way or the other." Nadia pulled out her phone and started typing notes.

"Wait," she said, "there's more. Look at this ad that keeps popping up before the video I need." On her screen, a basketball player Arthur recognized from the playoffs held up a sneaker and said everyone was wearing them this season. Arthur counted the tricks in his head. A famous athlete, a claim that everybody already had them, and the words " revolutionary" and "pathetic" in the on-screen text, describing the shoe and its rivals. "Athlete, bandwagon, loaded words," he said. "All three in fifteen seconds."

"It's like a simile that only goes one direction," Nadia said, tapping the screen. Arthur laughed, then opened a blank slide and typed the headline at the top. "Probable headline of our project," he said, reading it aloud: "How the Same Crowd Becomes Two Different Stories."

"The crowd was never two crowds," Nadia said, and hit save.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
story:
Emmett had one job at the mall: find a birthday gift for his grandmother while his mom picked up shoes at the other end. He had twenty dollars and forty minutes, and he was already wasting both at the phone repair kiosk, where his friend Rico worked weekends. His problem was simpler than it sounded. Grandmother had once mentioned a mug with a red fox painted on it, and Emmett could not remember where she had seen it. He pulled out his phone and typed his own name into the search box, on a hunch that he had once looked it up and saved the link.

The search results filled the screen, and near the top was something he did not expect: a comment he had written three years ago on the mall's public page, complaining about the arcade closing early on a Sunday. Anyone searching "Emmett" could read it, including strangers, and it even showed which mall location he had been at that day. He stared at it, then scrolled and found the same comment copied on a second site he had never visited.

"How is it on there twice?" he asked Rico, holding up the phone. "I only wrote it once."

Rico leaned over the counter. "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages," he said, wiping a smudge off the screen. "So anything posted publicly can turn up in search results." He shrugged, like it was just weather. "Even old stuff. Even with your name on it."

Emmett tested the idea right there. He found the original comment on the mall's page, edited it to conceal his last name and the location tag, and then searched again an hour later, while eating a pretzel by the fountain. The old copy on the second site still sat there, unedited, because he had no way to reach it. His own fix worked only halfway, and he understood now that a public post was less like a note passed in class and more like something pinned to a board anyone could photograph. He typed a fresh comment under the mall's post, asking if anyone knew a shop that sold fox mugs, using only his first initial this time.

The reply came while he was standing outside the pet store, watching a small owl blink at him from behind the glass. The sign said it was nocturnal, which explained why it looked half asleep under the bright mall lights, while the monitor lizard beside it, according to the sign a carnivore, tracked every movement near its tank with wide-open eyes. Emmett's phone buzzed. A stranger named Doris had answered: try the kitchenware shop on level two, third store past the escalator. He walked toward the escalator, reading the message a second time, and said, "Thanks, Doris," out loud to nobody in particular.

story:
Chase sat cross-legged on the floor of his aunt's guest room with a photocopy of the Havdalah blessing spread in front of him. In three weeks he would stand in front of ninety people at his Bar Mitzvah and recite it by heart, and right now he could not get past the fourth line. He tried again, mouthed the words, lost the thread, and flopped backward onto the rug.

Downstairs, his cousin Priya was arranging a plate of laddus on the kitchen counter. Her family had come to stay for the week after Grandpa Joe's funeral, and the house still smelled like casseroles and incense from two different traditions. Chase wandered in and slid the photocopy onto the counter. "How do you memorize a whole prayer? I keep forgetting the middle."

Priya tilted her head. "When my grandfather died last year, I learned a shloka for him. It took me eleven days." She tapped the paper. "It's gradual, like anything. One line locks in, then the next. My teacher says a neuron fires the same path every time you repeat something, and the path gets stronger."

"Eleven days," Chase groaned. "I have twenty-one." He stared at the page, then looked up. "Can I ask you something weird? Where do you think Grandpa Joe went? Like, actually went."

Priya set down the plate. "In Hinduism, the soul passes through samsara. That means a cycle of birth, death and rebirth, around and around." She traced a circle in the air with one finger. "And karma decides the direction. Karma is the results of a person's actions, and those results shape the next life."

Chase turned that over while he stole a laddu. A hidden rule, like gravity: you could not see it, only the effects. He wondered if it could be tested the way you test anything invisible, by watching what it did. "So if somebody was kind all the time, the kindness would... land somewhere?"

"That's the idea," Priya said. "Grandpa Joe gave my mom his winter coat the day they met. That kind of thing counts."

That night Chase tried something new. He drew the prayer as a circle instead of lines, arrows curving from each phrase to the next, so that the end flowed back to the beginning like Priya's finger in the air. When he forgot the middle, he could travel the loop the other way and arrive from the far side. By bedtime he had the whole thing, and the words no longer felt like a wall but like a path he had walked twice.

At the ceremony, three weeks later, he reached the fourth line and felt his mind go blank. He pictured the circle, traveled backward from the end, and the missing words appeared exactly where the arrows said they would be. He finished strong, and in the front row Priya drew a slow circle in the air.

story:
The assignment was due on Friday, and Landon had spent three days avoiding it. Now he sat in the school library at four o'clock, a blank page in front of him, and the clock above the biography shelves ticking like it was counting down a siege. He had to write a short story with dialogue, and the dialogue had to be punctuated right, and the whole thing needed a climax. Ms. Ferrante had circled his last attempt in red and written "See me" at the top, which was worse than any grade.

He tried a sentence. "Where are you going," He asked. It looked wrong the moment he wrote it, but he could not say why. His friend Priya slid into the chair across from him with her own paper and a granola bar. She leaned over his shoulder.

"Question mark," she said, tapping the page. Landon frowned. He flipped through the class packet of examples until he found one: "Where are you?" he asked. There it was, the question mark sitting inside the quotation marks, and the tag after it starting with a lowercase h. That seemed backwards to him. He asked was its own kind of sentence, wasn't it?

"Watch," Priya said. She took his pencil and wrote the whole thing out plain, without any marks: Where are you he asked. "Now decide where the question ends. Is He asked part of the question?" Landon stared at it. The question was only the part in the guy's mouth. The tag belonged to the narrator. He tried it both ways on the page, once with a capital H, once without, and read them aloud. The lowercase version sounded right, like one breath instead of two broken pieces. He erased the capital.

His old ideas for the story, a spaceship battle, suddenly felt dormant, like something that had been sitting too long in the dark. He had wanted a siege scene with robots. Instead he started writing about two brothers in a treehouse, one hiding something, and by the third line of dialogue he was writing fast, punctuating the questions without slowing down. Priya had moved on to her own paper, but when he read a line out loud she laughed once, quietly, and the librarian glanced over. Landon felt his ears go hot.

The problem was the climax. He wrote four versions where the brothers argued, and each one fizzled out. Then he tried having the younger brother finally ask the question he had been afraid to ask all story long: "Why didn't you come to Mom's funeral?" he asked. The older brother went silent on the page, and then Landon knew exactly what happened next, because the whole story had been waiting for that one question. He wrote the ending in a single sitting, twenty minutes, his hand cramped around the pencil.

When he read it through, though, the robot siege was gone for good, and he felt a small pang about that, the way you do when you trade something loud and fun for something quieter and harder. Priya packed up her bag and paused at his table. "Read it to me tomorrow before class?" she said. He slid the paper into his folder, smoothed the crease flat with his palm, and said, "Only if you fix my commas first."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
story:
Luca stood at the canoe launch with his duffel at his feet, waiting for the camp van, and tried to look like a kid who had done this a hundred times. He had never been to summer camp. His cousin Diego had spent a month at one last summer and came home telling stories about a lake, a rope swing, and something he called the frontier, a stretch of woods at the edge of the property where the older campers got to hike. Luca wanted that more than anything, and he'd said so on the ride up, so many times that his mom laughed. Now he watched the driver load his bag beside seven others and climbed in anyway.

The first week was good, until Tuesday night, when cabin inspection turned into tick check. The counselor handed each boy a flashlight and told them to line up, and a kid named Marcus groaned loudly. "We didn't even hike today. Why bother?" He flopped onto his bunk and pulled his sleeping bag over his head like a tent.

Luca had been scratching behind his knee since the afternoon trail walk, and while Marcus complained, he thought about it. He hadn't hiked Monday either, but today they had cut through a field of tall grass to reach the swimming dock, off the trail, because it was faster. The itching had started after that. He couldn't see the back of his own knee, but the fact of the itching was data, like a footprint. He grabbed the kid next to him, a quiet boy named Owen. "Can you check behind my knee with the flashlight? We went through that tall grass by the dock."

Owen shined the light and went still. "There's something there. Small. Like a poppy seed with legs." Luca's stomach dropped, but he made himself think instead of panic. Marcus peeked out from his sleeping bag, suddenly interested. "Is that a blacklegged tick?" he asked. "My sister got one at her camp. She said they're also called deer ticks, and they can spread Lyme disease, so everybody had to check every night."

"Then check everybody," Luca said, pulling his pant leg down. "Especially anyone who was in that grass." Marcus sat up, all complaints gone, and helped Owen run the flashlights along ankles and hairlines and behind ears. They found two more ticks among the six boys who had taken the shortcut, and the counselor got them off properly and logged it, while Marcus explained to the next cabin over why the nightly check existed. "I take back what I said," he told them. "This is the most sophisticated reason to make us line up I've ever heard."

By Friday, the whole cabin had a system. Lights out, then flashlights on, then a rotation where each boy checked the boy behind him, faster every night, until it consumed barely five minutes. "Efficient," Owen said, with a small proud smile, and Marcus gave Luca a fist bump. On Sunday, the frontier hike opened for the older campers, and Luca's name was on the list. He caught up to the group at the trailhead, boots already dusty, and Marcus tossed him a spare flashlight. "For after," Marcus said, and Luca grinned and tucked it in his pocket as they stepped into the trees.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
Georgia had one job at the polling station: hold her grandmother's place in line while Gran fetched her glasses from the car. But the line was slow, and beside the door somebody had taped up a poster of the town charter, all forty rights printed in tiny columns. Georgia started reading to pass the time.

She was halfway through the list, lips moving, when a man in a green jacket came out of the voting hall. She recognized him. Councillor Ruiz, the one from the newspaper photo. He had voted against the bylaw that banned skateboarding in the library plaza, the bylaw that had emptied the plaza and pushed every skater in Georgia's grade onto the cracked lot behind the gas station.

"You're Councillor Ruiz," she said. "You said the plaza ban was wrong. So when are you changing it?"

He smiled, but not much. "I can't change it alone. A single councillor can't change a bylaw alone. A change needs a majority vote of the whole council."

Georgia stared at him. "But you agree it's a bad rule."

"Agreeing isn't voting power. There are seven of us."

She looked back at the charter poster. Right there, near the top: the right of citizens to gather peacefully and to petition their government. She'd read it twice without really reading it. Now she said it out loud, slowly, testing it. "So we can ask. Together. That's not just a decoration on a wall."

"That's the idea," Ruiz said. "Petitions matter. Voters matter. Today, especially."

Georgia's mind was moving fast. This was polling day, and the whole town was walking past this door. People who cared enough to vote cared enough to sign something. That was the hidden pattern: the ban hadn't been defeated by one enemy, it had passed because nobody had shown up to argue, and now the people who could argue were all standing in one line. She ran to Gran's car, grabbed the notebook from the back seat, and tore out six pages.

"Sign here if you want the plaza bylaw reconsidered," she called, standing where everyone had to pass. A woman with a stroller signed. Two teenagers signed without asking questions. A man in a volatile mood, red-faced about parking tickets, refused, but then a library volunteer signed right after him and told him the plaza used to be full of kids before the ban. He scowled and kept walking, but slower.

By the time Gran came back with her glasses, Georgia had ninety-three signatures. Ninety-three, in one hour, from one line. She counted them twice on the bench by the door.

She had wanted Ruiz to fix it, one important person snapping his fingers. Now she wanted something different: seven votes, and a stack of paper heavy enough to matter. She folded the pages, squared them against her knee, and walked the stack straight back to Councillor Ruiz.

"You said majority," she told him. "So start counting."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Flight 47 to Phoenix was delayed again, and Florence spread her science homework across two plastic seats in the gate area. Her graph for the Sonoran Desert showed rainfall bars so short they looked like a typo, while the rainforest graph she'd copied from the library book had bars like a row of broken teeth, tall and constant. She had to compare them using temperature too, and the assignment sheet called for a paragraph she had not yet managed to formulate.

Her little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder with a topographic map of the mountain near Grandma's house. "You said we'd go sledding when we land," he said. "Pick the hill before Mom changes her mind."

"Mom already changed her mind twice," Florence said. "Once about the window seat."

The map was covered in wiggly brown lines, close together in some places and far apart in others. Checking each line against the height numbers printed on it was tedious, and Florence kept losing her place whenever the gate agent announced something nobody listened to. She traced one slope with her finger where the lines bunched up like angry eyebrows, then another where they were scattered wide, and a third where they marched down the page at regular intervals, like fence posts.

"That one," Theo said, poking the regular one.

"Why that one?"

He shrugged. "It looks calm."

Florence frowned. The lines on that slope were evenly spaced, each one the same distance from the last, all the way from the top of the hill to the creek. On the other slopes the spacing changed, tight then loose then tight again. She thought about what the spacing might be hiding, since the map could not show her the actual ground. Wide spacing had to be one steepness and narrow spacing another, so if the spacing never changed, then the steepness never changed either. "Contour lines spaced evenly apart," she said slowly, "show a slope that has the same steepness all the way along it."

"So no surprise cliffs?"

"No surprise cliffs." She drew a red circle around the slope and wrote GO HERE under it, then held the map up to the window. Beyond the tarmac, a fuel vessel sat parked beside the plane, and a man in orange ear protection was checking its gauge.

She turned back to her graphs, and now the comparison wrote itself almost without her. The desert's temperature line swung up and down with the seasons while rainfall stayed nearly nothing; the rainforest stayed warm and soaked month after month. Two places, two patterns, and you could read the whole climate off the shapes. She finished the paragraph, then looked at the clock and at the map.

"Forty minutes till boarding," she said. "Enough time to check the map for a backup hill, in case the first one is full of kids who also like calm."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
story:
Rachel's cousin Marcus had been holding court by the potato salad for ten minutes, and she was tired of it. "My coach's sister took that new cold syrup and was better in two days," he announced. "It works. Case closed."

"It's not closed," Rachel said. "That's one person. Grandma got over her cold last week with no syrup at all."

"Grandma is a tank," Marcus admitted, and half the picnic table laughed, because Grandma was currently beating Uncle Ray at arm wrestling.

Rachel wanted to settle it, and she had a tool: her science homework, an article about a real study of that exact syrup. She fetched the printout from the car, dodging Aunt Denise, who tried to delegate dish duty to her on the way past the kitchen window. "After," Rachel promised, which was what everybody said and nobody meant.

She read the article while Marcus chewed. The researchers had given the syrup to some people and a lookalike, tastelike nothing to others. What stopped her was one line: the people in the study hadn't chosen which one they got. They were assigned to their groups at random, like a coin flip, so that differences like age or health were likely to be spread evenly between the groups instead of piling up on one side. "Why random?" Marcus asked, spraying crumbs. "Why not let people just pick?"

Rachel thought about it, turning her cup around and around. "Because if volunteers picked, the healthy people might all grab the syrup, and then the syrup group would look great even if the syrup did nothing. If you flip the coin, both groups get the same mix." She looked up, pleased with herself, then less pleased. "Which means your coach's sister proves nothing. She just picked herself."

"So we test it," Marcus declared, undeterred. He stood on the picnic bench like a tiny general. "Everybody who had a cold this winter, raise a hand!"

Eleven hands went up. Rachel made two columns in her notebook, syrup and no syrup, and hunted down the details like a monsoon rolling through the party, relentless and slightly damp, since it started raining and she kept going anyway under the porch roof. Uncle Ray had taken the syrup and been sick for a week. Little Jo had taken nothing and bounced back in three days. Aunt Denise, Grandma, two second cousins, all with intricate stories of honey, soup, and one questionable sock soaked in vinegar.

The results were a beautiful, useless mess. Two of the syrup people got better fast, two didn't, and Grandma, still syrup-free, demanded to know why anyone would drink "that swamp water" when soup existed.

"So we learned nothing," Marcus said, flopping onto the bench beside her, rain dripping off his hair.

"We learned one thing," Rachel said. "Next time, we flip a coin first."

Grandma slammed down Uncle Ray's arm one final time and called across the yard, "That's my girl. Now somebody dry off the potato salad."

story:
The spelling bee was held in the back corner of the public library, between the biography shelves and a radiator that clanked like it had opinions. Sofia sat in the second row, mouthing words to herself. Her real problem was sitting in the first row: Marcus, whose cousin lived in Canada, and who had spent all week insisting that "colour" was the correct spelling and that Americans had ruined everything.

"Round three," announced the librarian, Ms. Okafor. "Sofia. Your word is 'condense'."

Sofia pictured steam turning to droplets on a cold window. "C-O-N-D-E-N-S-E. Condense."

"Correct." Ms. Okafor shuffled her cards, then paused. "Interesting. Round four will be our vocabulary bonus round. The word is 'arid'. Use it in a sentence to earn two extra points."

"Arizona is so arid that even the cactuses look thirsty," Sofia said, and half the audience laughed.

Marcus got "intestine," spelled it, and whispered, "You're going down," as he passed her chair. Then Ms. Okafor said the word Sofia had been dreading and hoping for at the same time.

"Colour."

The room went quiet. "Color," Sofia said slowly. "Or colour? Which country are we in?"

"Spellers may ask for the word's origin," Ms. Okafor said cheerfully.

"Origin, please."

"This spelling comes to English through French."

Sofia's brain spun. French spelling would be "colour," with the u. But Marcus kept saying his Canadian cousin spelled it that way, and Canada used British spellings, and they were not in Canada. She had a theory, and only one way to test it. "C-O-L-O-R. Color."

"Correct."

Marcus shot up from his seat. "That's wrong! My cousin Dara spells it colour! She says Americans just randomly dropped the u!"

Sofia marched to the reference shelf, pulled down the big dictionary, and flipped until she found the word history box beside "color." Marcus leaned over her shoulder, still fuming.

"Look at this," Sofia said. "Noah Webster's 1828 American Dictionary of the English Language promoted simpler spellings like color instead of colour. And those spellings became standard in the United States."

"So it wasn't random," Marcus said slowly.

"Nope. It was Webster. You can be mad at a person, which is way more satisfying."

Marcus studied the page, then grinned. "Fine. But Dara's still going to say Webster was wrong."

"Tell her to take it up with the radiator," Sofia said, and patted the clanking pipe like an old friend.

story:
Elijah got to the park ten minutes early, which he decided was exactly the wrong amount of early, because now he had time to think about everything that could go wrong. Maya was meeting him by the fountain at two. He had rehearsed a list of questions on the bus, and at the top of it was the one he was surest about: Do you like school?

She showed up right on time, and they walked to the coffee kiosk by the playground. He bought two hot chocolates even though it was eighty degrees out, because it was the first thing he'd planned and he couldn't think fast enough to change it.

"Do you like school?" he asked as they sat down on the bench.

Maya shrugged. "Yeah."

"Do you like this park?"

"Yeah. It's nice."

The conversation kept dying like that, question, one word, silence, question, one word, silence. Elijah could feel the afternoon leaking away. He stared at the fountain and tried to figure out what was happening. It wasn't that Maya didn't want to be there, he thought, because she kept glancing at him like she was waiting for something. The trouble seemed to be with the questions themselves, though he couldn't see that directly. He ran back through them. Do you like school. Do you like this park. Do you like hot chocolate. He noticed a pattern: every question he'd asked could be answered with a single word and then it was over, like a door that only opened one inch.

He decided to test it. "What's a class you'd take if school let you invent one?" he asked.

Maya put down her cup. "That's actually a good question. I'd take a class on propaganda, like how ads and posters get you to believe stuff without you noticing. My grandpa has all these old posters from a country that doesn't even exist anymore, and some of them are beautiful and completely terrifying." She talked for two whole minutes, and then she asked him a question back, and he elaborated on his answer about a class on haunted bridges until she was laughing so hard she nearly spilled her hot chocolate.

"Okay, your turn to answer the class one," she said, tapping his arm. "For real."

"A class on how to talk to people," he said. "Because apparently yes-or-no questions are terrible and I only just figured that out."

Maya stopped laughing and looked at him strangely, and for one long second he worried he'd said something wrong. Then she said, "Wait. You did that on purpose? You changed your questions halfway through?"

He nodded, bracing himself.

"That is the nerdiest, most impressive thing anyone has ever done on a date with me," she said, and grabbed the last of his hot chocolate, and pointed toward the playground. "Race you to the swings."

Eve slid her debate notes across the desk and checked the clock above the whiteboard. Fifteen minutes until her turn, and her argument still had a hole in the middle of it. The topic on the board read, "Why do two people watch the same event and walk away certain of different things?" Mr. Reyes had written it up that morning and refused to say more, which Eve thought was unfair, since the whole class kept raising their hands and he kept saying, "Work it out with each other."

"I'm saying the security camera settles it," Marcus whispered beside her. He wanted to win, that was plain; he'd said twice already that he never lost a debate. "The sensor over the gym door recorded the whole thing. Facts are facts."

"But my cousin Priya saw the fight from the bleachers, and she swears Deshawn shoved first," Eve said. "And my other cousin Jamal was standing right next to Deshawn, and he swears Deshawn only put his hands up." She looked down at her notes. Both cousins had been at the same family barbecue afterward, each one calling the other blind or stubborn, and Eve had spent the whole evening wondering how two honest people could end up so angry at each other over one hallway shoving match.

She flipped through her sister's psychology book, which she'd brought because the cover promised something about perception. There it was, a sentence she'd underlined the night before: naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased. She read it twice. That was Priya exactly, and it was Jamal too, and if she was honest, it was also her, sitting there certain that Priya was the reasonable one because Priya was her favorite cousin.

"Three minutes," Mr. Reyes called out.

Eve grabbed her pencil. She could incorporate the idea into her opening, right after the camera part, so Marcus's facts wouldn't collapse the moment she mentioned cousins. She scribbled fast, then tapped his arm. "You're doing it right now," she said. "You think the sensor footage is just the truth, so anybody who reads it differently must be dumb or lying. That has a name."

Marcus frowned at her notes. "So what, nobody can be wrong?"

"I don't know yet," Eve admitted. Behind them, Mr. Reyes stood and pointed at the clock.

"Eve and Marcus, you're up."

Marcus grabbed his cards. "Fine," he muttered, "but if the camera says I'm right, I'm saying so first."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
story:
Brooke had forty dollars of birthday money in her pocket and a plan: a new backpack from the mall's sporting goods store. But on the way, she passed the bank kiosk near the fountain, where a poster showed two lines climbing side by side over five years. Simple interest grew in a straight staircase. Compound interest curved upward, because each year's interest earned interest of its own. She stared at the graph until her cousin Dana elbowed her.

"You're doing money homework at the mall? Tragic," Dana said.

"There's a difference," Brooke said. She grabbed a flyer and a pen from the counter. "If I put forty dollars in at simple interest, I get the same flat amount every year. Compounding pays me on the whole balance, so it accelerates." She sketched five quick boxes on the back of the flyer, doubling her totals in her head, and the numbers diverged by year three. The compound line pulled away like the fast lane on the escalator.

Then she spotted a display card beside the poster: a corporate bond paying nearly twice the interest of the savings account. Twice. She turned to Dana. "Why would anyone pick the savings account? This is obviously better."

"Nothing's obviously better," Dana said. "When we got our apartment lease, Mom said the landlord had to accommodate her service dog or we'd walk. Landlords who want something from you have to give something up." Dana tapped the card. "So ask yourself what the borrower wants from you and what they're giving up."

Brooke frowned and pulled up a finance page on her phone, typing in the bond's name. The rating was far below the top grades. She read the entry twice. "These are called junk bonds," she said slowly. "Companies that are more likely to fail to pay have to offer higher interest to get anyone to lend to them. That's why it pays double. It's not free money, it's a warning sticker." The page also called them high-yield, which sounded glamorous until she remembered what the yield was compensating for.

"So what do you do?" Dana asked.

Brooke laid the flyer flat on the counter and made two columns. The savings account had a small, certain rate that compounded every year; the bond had a big rate attached to a borrower who might not pay her back at all. She thought of it like a variable in math class: one thing she could hold constant, and one thing that could swing either way. "The credible choice is the boring one," she said. "For now. Maybe when I have more than forty dollars, I can take one small risk."

She walked to the bank desk and asked the teller to open a savings account with compound interest, then fed her two twenties into the bill reader. The receipt printed with a balance of $40.00 and a date five years in the future, when the account would be worth more.

"Backpack?" Dana asked as they headed for the escalator.

"Next birthday," Brooke said, folding the receipt into her pocket. "This one's climbing the curve."

story:
Isla stood in the hallway with her back against the doorframe, holding a pencil flat on top of her head the way her dad always did. He wasn't home yet, so she reached up and made the little line herself, then stepped sideways to look. The mark was barely above the one from September. Barely. She measured the gap with her thumb and it was about the width of an eraser.

Her brother Theo came thudding down the stairs with a folder under his arm. He'd had his knee checked at the doctor's that morning, and he was still telling everyone about it. "They took pictures of my bones," he said. "Actual pictures. Like the bones are glowing."

"X-rays," Isla said. "Everyone's seen those."

"Not of me." He flopped onto the couch and pulled out a dark film, holding it up to the window light. Long pale bones, and near the ends of them, thin darker gaps. Isla leaned in. She'd assumed bones grew from the middle, like a plant shooting up from its stem, but the gaps were all up near the joints.

"That's where they grow," Theo said. "The doctor called them growth plates. Right near the ends." He tapped the film with one finger. "And he said once they close after puberty, that's it, you're done getting taller. He pointed right at mine." He sounded proud, like the closing plates were a trophy.

Isla sat down slowly on the arm of the couch. Done getting taller. She thought about the eraser-width of growth in three months, and about how her jeans from last spring still fit, even though her shoes had gone up a whole size. Her body was clearly doing something, but not the something she wanted. There was no way to see a growth plate on her own legs, no way to peek. But there was the doorframe, with its pencil lines going back to kindergarten, and the date written beside each one. That was her evidence, her pattern, the only record she had.

She went and got the notebook where she tracked everything, hurricane names and homework and now this, and copied the heights onto graph paper. September, October, November, December. The line climbed, small but steady, not flat, not finished. She decided to keep the marks monthly, first Sunday of each, and to exclude any measurement taken with shoes on, since that would ruin the data.

"You're being weird," Theo said, watching her draw.

"I'm being scientific." She snapped the elastic band off the notebook and used it to hang her pencil on a nail beside the doorframe, so it would always be there. Outside, the first thunder of the monsoon season rolled in, and rain started hammering the roof.

"Measure me too," Theo said, getting up. "Right now, before dinner."

Isla pressed the pencil flat against his head and drew the line. "Say the date."

"May eighteenth," Theo said, and she wrote it underneath.

story:
Grandpa's porch was the best place in the world to figure things out, and Colton had a big thing to figure out before Monday. His cousin Marcus was visiting too, along with a neighbor kid named Theo, and Grandpa had promised them all lemonade and a chess set older than anyone in the room.

Theo was quiet and wore the same dinosaur shirt two days in a row, which gave Marcus all the material he needed. "Nice shirt," Marcus said, grinning. "Did you dig it out of a museum?"

Theo's comeback was fast and clever. "At least I don't look like a potato with eyebrows."

Colton actually laughed before he could stop himself, and Theo's face went red. Marcus didn't laugh back, though. He leaned forward like a hawk spotting something small and helpless, which was exactly the predatory look the older kids at school got right before things got loud. "A potato with eyebrows?" Marcus said. "Okay, fossil boy. Does your mom still cut your hair with a bowl?"

"Does yours cut yours with a weed whacker?"

By the third round, Theo was shouting, Marcus was shouting, and the chessboard sat forgotten. Colton realized he was watching the exact pattern from school. Last week a kid named Ryan had teased a classmate named Dev, and Dev had fired back a brilliant insult about Ryan's shoes. He'd expected applause. story:
Riley set her debate packet on the library table so hard that the pages fanned out like a dropped deck of cards. Her assignment sheet said, in Ms. Okafor's looping handwriting, "Thesis and three-point outline before any draft. No exceptions." Riley had a draft already, two pages of it, written last night in one long sprint about why the school should start a recycling program. The problem was that her draft said three different things, and she could not tell which one she actually believed.

Across the table, her friend Devon was marking up an essay with a green pen, circling words one by one. Riley watched him fix "recieve" to "receive" and "there" to "their" and move a comma.

"Is that revising?" she asked.

"Yep," Devon said. "Revised it twice already."

Riley slid her laptop toward him. "Can you look at mine, then? Just tell me what to fix."

He read for a minute, then turned the screen back to her. "There's like one spelling error. Congrats. But your first paragraph says recycling saves money, your second says it saves the planet, and your third says it teaches responsibility, and then they all just kind of wander off."

Riley exhaled slowly and stared at the ceiling tiles. "So if fixing spelling is revising, what's this other thing called, where I have to take my own argument apart?"

Devon shrugged. "My tutor says the word 'revise' comes from the Latin revisere, meaning 'to look at again'." He went back to his green pen. "So real revising is supposed to be seeing the draft again, like a civilian who never met you, not fixing typos like a machine."

A civilian who never met you. Riley sat with that. She opened a new document and typed one sentence at the top: "The school should fund a recycling program because it saves money, builds student responsibility, and sets an example for the district." Then she made three headings and dragged chunks of her draft under each one. Under "saves money," she found she had almost no evidence, just enthusiasm. Under "responsibility," she found her strongest paragraph, the one about the sixth graders who ran the cafeteria compost bins. Interesting, she thought. The outline was like a map of her own brain, and apparently her brain had been marching in three parallel directions at once.

She deleted her entire second point. It hurt a little, like throwing away a drawing she'd spent an hour on, but the map was clearer with two roads instead of three, so she split the responsibility point into two halves and rebuilt.

At 3:45 Devon packed up. "How's the typo situation?" he asked.

"Extremely bad," Riley said. "I just cut two hundred words and moved everything." She turned the screen toward him. "But I looked at it again. First time, actually."

He leaned in, read the new outline top to bottom, and laughed. "Riley. Your thesis says the program saves money."

"It does."

"Your evidence is a compost bin run by sixth graders."

Riley looked at her outline, really looked, and the flaw opened up under her eyes like a pothole. "Okay," she said, cracking her knuckles. "Round two."

story:
Laurence knelt on the stone floor of the temple annex with a folded sheet of Sanskrit verses in front of her. In three weeks she would chant the whole prayer from memory in front of the congregation, part of her coming-of-age ceremony, and so far she could get through four lines before the words slipped away from her.

Her cousin Priya found her there after the morning bells. "You look like you're trying to stare a hole in the paper," Priya said.

"It won't stick. I read it over and over and it just slides off." Laurence flattened the page against the floor. "How did you ever memorize anything for your ceremony?"

Priya sat down beside her. "I didn't memorize for that. I danced. Two hours a day for four years, and last spring I finally did my first full solo performance. It's called an arangetram. It means ascending the stage." She straightened the edge of her shawl. "It marks the end of my first formal training."

Laurence looked at her. "Four years. And you're still the one who complains about practice."

"Exactly because of that." Priya laughed.

That night Laurence thought about the difference between Priya's four years and her own three weeks. Priya hadn't learned her dance by reading it. She had learned it with her feet and her hands, the same movements repeated until her body knew them without the mirror. Laurence had been treating the prayer as something on paper, a thing outside her, instead of something she could carry in her mouth and her breath.

The next morning she tested the idea. She stood in the temple courtyard, left the sheet folded in her pocket, and chanted the first line while touching the pillar nearest the door, the way she had done on her first day. Then the second line at the tulsi planter, the third at the low step. She walked the route six times, tying each line to a place she could walk to.

On the sixth round, her aunt tried to intervene, saying she should come in and eat before the priest arrived, but Laurence held up one hand and finished the verse at the bell rope without a single mistake.

At breakfast her uncle asked why she was grinning at her idli. "I thought memorizing meant being biased toward my eyes," she said. "All reading, no doing. I was wrong. It's in my feet now too." Nobody in the family had paid a single rupee for lessons, unlike Priya's parents, whose income had stretched thin over four years of dance fees, and that made the walking method even better.

On the day of the ceremony she stood before the congregation, closed her eyes, and saw the courtyard in her mind, pillar, planter, step, bell rope. Her voice moved from station to station. When she finished, she opened her eyes, and Priya, in the second row, raised her hands in a dancer's salute.

story:
The onion came out of the root cellar still cold, and Oliver peeled a single layer of skin from its curved side with tweezers, the way the science booklet said, laying it flat on a glass slide. His grandfather's microscope sat on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a jar of bolts. It had been in the barn loft for years, and Oliver had spent half the morning polishing its little mirror before he could see anything at all.

He wanted this to work. He had written to his grandfather three weeks ago, when the science fair project was assigned, asking if he could borrow the microscope, and yesterday a letter had finally come back. The letter was in his pocket now, soft at the folds from being read too many times. His grandfather wrote about the farm and the weather, and then, near the end, about a summer long ago when he had volunteered in the Galápagos Islands counting finches. That part Oliver had read four times.

First, though, he had to see the cells. He dropped a bead of water and a thread of iodine onto the skin, pressed the cover slip down, and bent to the eyepiece. At first there was only a pale blur. He turned the knob a fraction at a time, the way a careful person turns a key in an old lock. Then the blur sharpened into rows of brick-like cells, each one walled off from the next, and there inside each cell, faintly, a dark dot.

He sat back. He found the diagram in his booklet and matched it piece by piece. The thick outer line of every brick was the cell wall. Just inside it, so thin he could barely tell it apart, was the membrane. The dark dot was the nucleus. He labeled them on his own drawing, and where he could not decide whether a line was wall or membrane, he guessed, and the guess felt arbitrary, so he checked it twice.

Then he took out the letter. "You asked once whether bigger is always better," his grandfather had written. "On the island of Daphne Major, the medium ground finches had big beaks, good for big hard seeds. But after the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds, selection reversed, and smaller beaks were favoured." Oliver read it again, thinking of his grandfather the year he sold the big tractor and bought the small one, and how the neighbors had laughed, and how nobody laughed after the dry summer. He looked back into the eyepiece at the little walled city, every cell the same size, nobody bigger than anybody.

The screen door banged and his mother came in with two buckets of feed. "You find them?" she asked.

"Wall, membrane, nucleus," he said, and slid the letter across the table to her, still open to the last page.

story:
The kitchen smelled like burnt garlic, and Easton was trying to write an essay at the table while his cousin Mira practiced tinikling between the counter and the fridge. She had two wooden spoons and was tapping them on the floor, and her friend Daisy was stepping in and out of them like her ankles were made of glass. "Tap, tap, clap," Mira counted, loud and nervous, because in the real dance two people tapped bamboo poles on the ground twice and then clapped them together on the third beat, and if Daisy miscounted, the spoons would snap shut on her ankles like a cranky turtle.

"Can you count quieter?" Easton asked.

"Can you write quieter?" Mira said. "Your pencil sounds like a rebellious squirrel."

Easton looked down at his paper. The assignment was to compare how two faiths explained what happens after death, and he had exactly two sentences, one of which was his name. His lola believed in heaven and purgatory, which she described as being made clean before you went home. His friend Tomas's family was Buddhist and talked about being reborn, coming around again in a different form. Both ideas were about something nobody could actually see and come back from to report, which struck Easton as the world's worst homework design.

Then Daisy yelped. Mira had gotten excited on a turn and clapped the spoons a beat early, catching Daisy's sock. Daisy hopped on one foot, laughing, and Mira covered her face. "I'll embarrass myself at the recital," she groaned into her hands.

"No, wait," Easton said, standing up. "Count out loud, like you were doing. You kept her ankles clear when you counted. It went wrong when you stopped counting."

Mira gave him a suspicious look but started again. "Tap, tap, clap. Tap, tap, clap." Daisy's feet flicked in and out, safe every time, like the pattern was a law of nature instead of two wooden spoons.

Easton sat back down and looked at his blank page, and something clicked that felt like a spoon clapping shut. Both beliefs were patterns too, ways of counting past something you couldn't see. His lola's way said you went home after being made clean. Tomas's way said you came around again, like the third beat returning to the first. He couldn't test either one, not the way he'd just tested Mira's counting, but he could set them side by side and watch where they matched and where they clashed. His pencil finally started moving.

"Done!" Daisy announced, arms up like a champion.

"Tap, tap, clap," Easton read aloud from his page, then scribbled a new first line: Life, life, and then what?

story:
Kayla stood at Grandma Rosa's counter with an onion the size of a softball and a knife she was slightly afraid of. Her older cousin Marco always chopped the onions at family dinners, and everyone laughed about how he cried through every sauce. This year Kayla had asked to learn, and now here she was, being shown how to curl her fingers into a claw, knuckles forward, so the blade could only find the vegetable and never her fingertips.

"Watch," Grandma said, tucking her own hand into the same claw shape. "The knuckles are the wall. The knife rides along them." Kayla copied it, feeling a little like a crab. Her first cut was crooked, but the second was straighter, and by the fifth she noticed a pattern: the closer the tip of the knife stayed to the board, the less the onion slipped. She wondered if that was true for every vegetable, or just onions with their slick skins.

The sauce came together piece by piece. Onions into the oil, then garlic, then the tomatoes Grandma had crushed by hand. Kayla tasted it and frowned. "It needs something," she said. "I want to revise it. More salt? A pinch of sugar?" Grandma slid the sugar jar across the counter without a word, which Kayla took to mean she'd guessed right.

The problem arrived with the rice. Grandma's timer went off while the bread still had ten minutes in the oven, and there was no free burner, because the sauce was bubbling away on the last one. Grandma reached to lift the pot and hesitated. Kayla called her friend Priya, who cooked dinner at her house every Thursday. "Take it off the heat," Priya said, "lid on. It can rest like that for several minutes and the trapped steam finishes it. That frees the stove for other dishes." Kayla reported it, and Grandma raised an eyebrow, wiped her hands, and moved the pot to a cold burner with the lid pressed down tight.

While the bread finished, Grandpa wandered in still taking his antibiotic for his chest, so Kayla pushed the orange juice away from him and poured him water instead. He watched her stir the sauce and asked what was in it, and she told him: onion, garlic, hand-crushed tomatoes, one secret pinch of sugar. She kept glancing at the rice pot, wondering what was happening under that lid that she couldn't see. Was it really still cooking, or just sitting there? When she finally lifted the lid, the grains stood plump and separate, steam curling up past her face. "It worked," she said. Grandma tasted a forkful, nodded, and pointed at the pasta water, which had just begun to boil.

The last chocolate chip cookie on the cafeteria table was about to cause a war. Rachel watched Danny wave two dollars over it while Priya held up three, and behind them a sixth grader was digging through a backpack with the focus of someone defusing a bomb.

"Sold to Priya for three dollars," said Marcus, who ran the bake sale table like a small corporation. He had one cash box, one price list, and no interest in fairness. Yesterday the same cookies had been fifty cents each, because yesterday there had been forty of them.

"That's not right," Danny said afterward, walking with Rachel down the hall. "The seller just picks whatever number he wants. Marcus decided three dollars."

"Priya decided three dollars," Rachel said. "She offered it. If nobody wanted cookies, Marcus would be giving them away by lunch."

They argued all the way to the library, where Rachel was supposed to be documenting sources for her social studies paper. Instead she typed "who sets prices" into the catalog, mostly to win the argument. One thin green book came up, and she pulled it off the shelf and sat on the floor between the stacks to read it.

"Listen to this," she called to Danny, who had followed her in. "Some economist, Alfred Marshall, wrote it in 1890 in his book 'Principles of Economics.' He said supply and demand are like the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price."

"So neither one alone does it," Danny said slowly.

"So we were both kind of right, which is the worst possible outcome." Rachel checked the page again to make sure she had the year right, because Danny was famous for claiming her sources were biased whenever they supported her side. 1890. The book said 1890. The scissors had been around a long time, cutting prices in half with two blades, and nobody at their lunch table had noticed.

The next morning Rachel brought a test. She baked a dozen cookies at home, with her mother supervising the oven part, and set them next to Marcus's table with a sign that said ONE DOLLAR. Marcus sneered at her amateur operation until fourth period, when his own cookies ran out and hers were the only ones left in the building. By lunch, kids were offering her two dollars, then two fifty, and one boy tried to reserve a cookie by paying in advance, which Rachel declined on the grounds that she was not a bank.

Then came the twist. At the end of lunch, Mr. Okafor, the vice principal, stopped at her table. Rachel braced for a lecture about unauthorized food sales. Instead he bought her last two cookies for three dollars and asked if she would be interested in running the snack table at the spring fundraiser, since last year's organizer had graduated.

"Fundraiser prices go up when it's a big crowd, right?" Rachel said, sliding him his change.

Mr. Okafor looked at her over the cookie. "Who have you been talking to?"

"A dead economist," Danny said, taking another dollar from a kid who had come back for seconds.
