story:
Lydia leaned over the lab table in room 214, where the radiator hissed because someone had turned the valve the wrong way and steam kept escaping into the already humid September air. In front of her lay two printed climate graphs, one for Cairo and one for Singapore, and Mr. Ruiz had asked the class to decide which place got more rain. The bars for Cairo looked taller in three different months, and Lydia tapped the paper triumphantly.

"See? Cairo wins in March, April, and May," she told Marcus, who sat across from her with his arms crossed. "The bars are right there. Taller means more."

Marcus frowned. "Singapore is a rainforest. My cousin went there and said it rained every single afternoon. Cairo is a desert. Deserts are dry, that's the whole point." He slid the papers closer to himself as if the graph might confess.

"You can't argue with a graph," Lydia said, but a small doubt hindered her from saying it too loudly. Deserts were dry. She knew that. She pulled both sheets back and looked again, not at the bars this time but at the numbers running up the left side of each page. On Cairo's graph, the rainfall axis climbed to 300 millimeters at the top. On Singapore's, it climbed to 400. She found March on both. Cairo's tall bar stopped at about 40. Singapore's shorter-looking bar, on its much taller axis, stopped at 170.

"Oh no," she said. "Look at the axes. The bars aren't on the same scale." She turned the papers so Marcus could see. "A short bar can stand for more rain if the axis goes higher. You can only compare the bars by height if both graphs use the same scale."

Marcus leaned in, traced the numbers with his finger, and sat back slowly. "So Singapore gets more rain in March. A lot more."

"And every other month too," Lydia said, checking the rest of the year and finding the same thing over and over. She had been so sure, and she had been wrong in front of the whole table group. Priya, two seats down, had heard everything and was already whispering it to someone else.

Mr. Ruiz walked by and set a small stack of fresh worksheets on their table, graphs with matching scales printed on both. "Try these," he said, and moved on.

Lydia took the top sheet, but she kept the old ones too, folded into her binder. She wanted to remember being certain and wrong at the same time, so next time she would look at the numbers before she pointed at the bars. "Fine," she told Marcus. "Your cousin's afternoons were right."

"Want to tell Priya that?" Marcus asked.

Lydia looked over at Priya, still whispering, and shook her head. "I'll tell her myself at lunch."

"your brain just keeps saying run." She laughed a small, real laugh and said her mom kept an optimistic sticky note on the fridge that she'd started ignoring.

Friday came. Tasha went second to last, and she stood there with her note card shaking, and she read the first slide, and then the second, and after the axolotl regrowing limbs she looked up and saw Priya mouthing "whoa" in the front row. When she sat down she texted Noah from across the room: "that was awful and i did it anyway." He wrote back, "memoir title. 'awful and i did it anyway.' you're welcome." On the walk to lunch she caught up with him at the water fountain, still pale but grinning. "Next one," she said, "I'm going third."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
story:
Elizabeth dragged the garden hose across the backyard and pointed it at the sandbox her little brother Caleb had claimed as his kingdom. He stood on the ladder of the slide with his arms crossed.

"That's my city," he said. "I'm the tenant. I pay rent in candy."

"You're squatting," Elizabeth said. "Move your buildings." She had a science project due Monday: she was supposed to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, using erosion and deposition, and she refused to just read a paragraph off the internet. She wanted to build the thing.

Caleb slid down and started relocating his plastic dinosaurs while she raked the sand into a smooth slope and turned the hose to a trickle. At first nothing happened. The water spread out and vanished. She narrowed the stream with her thumb and persisted, holding it in the same channel for ten minutes, and a small groove began to cut. Sand lifted from the upstream edge and traveled, then dropped where the flow slowed at the bottom, building a fan-shaped delta. She felt a jolt of recognition. Erosion on one end, deposition on the other, the canyon creeping backward between them. If a trickle did this in ten minutes, a river over millions of years made the carving inevitable.

"But it doesn't matter," Caleb said, kneeling to inspect her groove. "My rocks don't change. This gray one has been gray forever. Rocks are rocks."

"That's wrong," Elizabeth said. She held up two sandbox stones, one smooth, one jagged. She rubbed them together and grit fell onto the sand, the same grit the water was already carrying away. The jagged stone was becoming sand, and sand could press into new rock, and rock could melt or get squeezed and heated until it was something else entirely.

"Any rock can become any other rock," she said. "Melting, weathering, heat and pressure. It's called the rock cycle."

"You're making that up."

"Look it up yourself." She turned the hose back on, and the water found her groove again, deepened it, and split around a buried rock, leaving it standing on a little column of sand like a tiny mesa. Caleb watched the delta spread toward his last dinosaur.

"That's going to flood my guy," he said.

"Then move him. That's what the river does. It doesn't knock."

story:
Chase had one goal for the field trip to the Harlow Living History Farm: get through the day without his group's egg basket ending up on the ground. So far, so good. The morning had revolved around chores, and Mrs. Teller had assigned him, Priya, and Milo to the chicken coop, where a dozen hens strutted around like they owned the county.

"Collect the eggs, handle them gently, and bring them to the kitchen porch," the guide had said. Milo immediately dropped his clipboard, which did not inspire confidence.

Chase crouched in the straw, sliding his hand under a speckled hen who squawked at him like he was a parasite who had come to drink her blood. "Easy," he muttered. "I'm not even hungry." Priya snickered behind him, and the first egg went into the basket without incident. By the fourth, Chase felt like a professional.

Milo, holding two eggs up to the light like precious gems, suddenly frowned. "Hey. There's no rooster anywhere. I've been watching. Zero roosters. So if we keep these eggs somewhere warm, will they hatch?"

Chase considered the question while a hen pecked at his shoelace. No rooster, that was true. He tried to picture it: twenty eggs under a heat lamp, and one morning, twenty chicks. Something about it felt wrong, like a vending machine with nothing stocked inside. "I don't think so," he said slowly. "My grandma's neighbor has hens and no rooster, and she sells the eggs as eating eggs. If they hatched, she'd basically be running a chick factory for free."

"So what's the difference?" Milo demanded. "Eggs are eggs."

"Maybe not." Chase looked around the coop again, checking rafters, checking the yard through the wire. The hens were the whole population. An idea formed, simple enough to test. "Every chicken we've seen today came out of an egg. If these eggs could hatch on their own, the farm wouldn't need to buy chicks ever, right? But the guide said they order chicks in the spring."

Priya gasped. "She did! I wrote it down. I write everything down." She flipped her notebook open to a page with the words CHICKS ARRIVE, APRIL underlined twice.

Milo looked personally betrayed by biology. "So without a rooster, the eggs can't hatch into chicks at all?"

"That's my theory," Chase said. "Hens lay them either way. Rooster or no rooster, you still get eggs. But no rooster, no chicks. Ever."

They carried the basket to the kitchen porch, where the guide was demonstrating an old butter churn, its wooden lid so clouded and opaque with age that nobody could see inside. Milo set the eggs down with exaggerated ceremony, like a funeral.

"Good work," the guide said. "Those go to the frying pan tomorrow. We'll have a demonstration about breakfast in the 1800s."

Milo opened his mouth, closed it, and finally said, "So if I had kept one in my hoodie, nothing would ever happen. No matter what."

"Nothing," Chase confirmed, "except you'd smell like egg."

Priya raised her hand anyway, notebook at the ready. "One question. If hens lay eggs no matter what, then what exactly does the rooster do all day?"

From somewhere beyond the barn came a sound that was definitely not a cow.

story:
The train swayed through pine hills, and Elena's little sister Dory kept her fist closed tight on the seat between them. Their family trip was almost over, and Dory had been quiet since they left the park, which was not like her at all.

"Let me see it," Elena said. Dory tried to evade her eyes, staring out the window instead, but slowly she opened her fingers. In her palm sat a chunk of rose quartz, streaked with pink, about the size of a plum.

"Isn't it gorgeous? I found it right by the waterfall. The waterfall was the climax of the whole trip, and this is like a souvenir of it." Dory cupped her other hand over the stone. "It's mine now."

An affluent-looking man across the aisle glanced over the top of his newspaper, and Elena lowered her voice. Something was nagging at her, a memory she couldn't quite see. At the visitor center there had been a display, and the ranger had said the words on it out loud, but Elena had been too busy looking at the wolf skull to pay attention. She thought back. The words had come in a list, she was almost sure, and the list had been long enough to fill a whole poster. She dug through her backpack, pushing aside granola bar wrappers until her fingers found a folded paper: a brochure she had grabbed because it had a picture of a marmot on the front.

She unfolded it on the tray table. There it was, exactly as she remembered, a list of seven principles under the heading Leave No Trace. She read down the numbered lines. Plan ahead and prepare. Travel and camp on durable surfaces. Dispose of waste properly, which explained the ziplock bag of orange peels their dad had carried out. Then the fourth line: leave what you find.

"Seven of them," Elena said, tapping the page. "And number four says leave what you find. That rock belongs there, Dory. If everybody took one, there wouldn't be any left."

Dory's chin wobbled. "But I want to remember the waterfall."

"You can remember it another way. Remember the junior ranger badge you wanted so bad?" Elena leaned closer. "A ranger's job is following these rules. If you take the rock, you can't really call yourself one."

Dory stared at the stone for a long moment, then at the brochure. "Fine," she whispered. "But I'm drawing it first. Every single stripe." She pulled her sketchbook from under the seat and flattened it against the window, and Elena handed her a pencil.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
story:
Isaac sat in the back seat with his knees pressed against the driver's seat in front of him, which had never happened before this summer. Last year his legs had fit the car the way they always had. Now, on the drive to his grandmother's house, he kept shifting because his sneakers jammed into the seat pocket, and when he pulled his knee up to sit cross-legged, his shorts rode up and he saw them: thin lines, pale pink, running sideways across the skin above his knee like tiny scratches that had never bled.

"Stop wiggling," his sister Maya said beside him. She was eleven and had claimed the window seat, an argument Isaac had lost that morning and was still evaluating. Maybe he should have let her have the middle instead. Three hours of a wedged elbow was worse than forty minutes of no window.

"What are those?" Maya asked, pointing at his knee. "Is that a rash?"

"It's not a rash." Isaac bent closer. He turned his leg toward the light from the window. The lines were on both knees, he discovered, almost exactly matched, and he had not fallen, not scraped anything, not even gone through the blackberry bushes behind the gym. So they had come from inside somehow. He thought about his cousin Theo, who was fifteen and had lines kind of like these on his shoulders, and about how Theo had shot up four inches in a single season of basketball. Isaac had grown two shoe sizes since spring. Maybe that was it. Maybe when you grew too fast, the skin got left behind, like a note arriving after you'd already moved.

"I have them too," Maya said suddenly, in a smaller voice. She tugged her waistband down a half inch at her hip. "Right there. I thought something was wrong with me. I've been hiding them at the pool."

Isaac studied hers. Hers were fainter than his, thin pale streaks. "Those are stretch marks," he said. "From growing fast." He remembered then, on his own thigh, marks from two years ago when he'd had his first big growth spurt. He pulled up his shorts to check. You could barely find them now, just ghost-smudges in the light. "Look, my old ones mostly went away. They fade."

Maya inspected his leg, then hers, comparing. In the front seat their dad reached over and tapped the thermostat down two degrees because the sun had shifted onto his arm. "Everything okay back there?" he asked.

"Fine," Maya said, and pulled her waistband back up. "Isaac, tell me again about the fading part when we stop. Slowly. I want to remember it at the pool on Monday."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
story:
Zack sat at the corner table in the school library, a blank page in front of him and twenty minutes until the writing lab closed. His social studies essay was due Monday, and the assignment sheet said he had to state a thesis and outline a three-point argument before drafting a single paragraph. He had picked his topic, that the town should build a bike trail along Miller Creek, but every time he tried to start, his mind went as barren as the empty parking lot outside the window.

He flipped through a folder of sample essays Ms. Okafor had left on the shelf. One was about why the school day should start later, and it moved smoothly from one idea to the next. Another, about school uniforms, was choppy; each paragraph sat alone, like separate islands. Zack read them twice and noticed something. The smooth essay kept using small words at the start of its paragraphs: first, however, furthermore, therefore. The choppy one hardly used any. He set the two essays side by side and traced the words with his pencil. First introduced the opening point. However signaled a turn. Furthermore added something on top. Therefore showed what followed from everything before.

His friend Priya dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of books. "What are you doing, playing connect the dots?"

"Sort of." He slid the choppy essay toward her. "Read this paragraph, then the next one."

She frowned. "They don't go together. It's like the writer teleported."

"Now read it this way." He had copied a paragraph onto scratch paper and added one word at the start, furthermore. Priya read it again and her eyebrows lifted.

"Oh, that's better. Ms. Okafor calls those transition words."

Zack pulled his own paper back and built his outline. Thesis: the town should build the Miller Creek trail. Point one: the census counted four hundred more kids in town than five years ago, so the parks were crowded. Point two: the trail would keep riders off the busy road. Point three: the creek path was already public land, so the cost would be low. Then he added his connectors. First, the town has grown. However, the roads were never widened. Furthermore, the land is free. Therefore, the trail should be built.

He wrote the opening paragraph, and for the first time the sentences came out in order, each one pointing to the next. When the librarian flicked the lights twice, Zack packed his bag slowly, reading the outline one more time on his way to the door.

"Monday, I'm actually ready," he told Priya, and he held up the page so she could see the four little words circled in the margin.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
story:
The stopwatch came from a drawer marked obsolete equipment, and it looked the part, with a crack across the face and buttons worn smooth. Emily pressed it anyway, because the class had only five working stopwatches and fourteen students, and Marcus had claimed the good ones for his group within four seconds of the bell.

The plan was simple. Emily would release a marble from the top of the lab ramp, and Josh would stand at the end of the hallway, twenty meters away, and shout "go" the moment it left her hand. Then he would click the stopwatch when the marble crossed the tape line by his shoes. They would divide distance by time, quantify the speed, and draw the distance-time graph Mr. Patel wanted by Friday.

The first run gave them a speed of 0.4 meters per second, which would have been fine for a snail, possibly the only organism slower than their marble. They tried again. 0.38. Again. 0.41.

"That marble is not that slow," Emily said, staring at the numbers. Something was hiding in the setup, something they could not see. She paced off the hallway, counting tiles. Twenty meters, same as before. The ramp angle hadn't changed. The only thing between her and Josh was air.

Then she remembered the lesson from last week, the one about sound. Warm air carried it faster than cold air, gaining about 0.6 meters per second for each degree Celsius. If the hallway was warm, Josh's "go" reached her quickly, but on a cold day it would crawl, and her start would be late, which would make the marble seem slow. She checked the thermometer by the door: 26 degrees. She did the arithmetic on her palm with a pencil. At 20 meters, a small delay in hearing "go" added a real chunk of error to every run.

They tested it. Emily had Josh clap hard against the far wall and timed the echo with the cracked stopwatch, once in the warm hallway by the radiators and once in the cold stairwell, ten trials each. The warm trials came back faster, and when she worked the numbers, the difference matched the rule: about 0.6 meters per second for every degree. She drew the graph with corrected times, and the line came out clean and steep and beautiful.

Mr. Patel walked past and squinted at it. "Nice correction for sound delay. Next time, use the light gate instead of shouting. Light doesn't dawdle."

"Light doesn't dawdle," Josh repeated, nodding, and packed up his stopwatch.

Emily carried the ramp back to the shelf. "One question," she said. "When I released the marble, when exactly did you start timing?"

Josh adjusted his backpack strap. "Right after I heard 'go.' Well. After 'go' and one Mississippi. Mr. Patel said always count one Mississippi."

Emily looked at her beautiful graph, then at Josh, then at the drawer of obsolete equipment, which suddenly seemed like the most honest thing in the room. "Give me the stopwatch," she said.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
Eve stood in the kitchen with her hands pressed flat against her sides, whispering the words of the blessing she had to know by Sunday. Her grandmother had written it out for her in careful looping ink, and on Sunday, at the ceremony, she would say it alone in front of the whole family. She had to know it by heart.

The problem was her arms. Every time she reached a tricky line, her hands flew up without asking her, as if they could pull the next word out of the air. She'd clamp them down and lose her place. She tried again in the hallway, and her right hand escaped on "bless the road before me." She growled and started over.

Her cousin Fiona came in carrying her dance bag. "You look like you're being electrocuted."

"I'm memorizing."

"Arms down," Fiona said. "In Irish step dancing, that's the rule. Arms still, feet fast." She dropped into position, hands pressed to her sides, and her shoes hammered out a rhythm on the floorboards, heels and toes chasing each other while her shoulders never moved. It looked almost impossible, like two different people sharing one body.

Eve watched her and a question started forming. Her arms flapped when her brain was hunting for a word. Fiona's feet worked fast while her body stayed quiet. What if the flapping wasn't the problem? What if it was just energy with nowhere to go? Maybe it didn't matter which part of her moved, as long as something did.

"Play the reel," she said. "The slow one you practice to."

Fiona raised an eyebrow but found it on her phone. The fiddle started, infectious even at practice speed, and Eve planted her feet and began the simple steps Fiona had taught her last summer, the ones where you never lift your arms. On the third try, the whole blessing came out in order, word after word, her hands glued to her sides the entire time.

She tried it again to be sure. Then once more without music, just her feet marking time on the tiles. It held.

"Percentage of how sure you are?" Fiona asked.

"Ninety. Ninety-five."

"Grandma's going to ask how you did it. You going to disclose your secret method?"

Eve grinned and didn't answer. She started the steps again, hands pressed to her sides, and the first line of the blessing came out steady and strong.
